sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Users list items in timed auctions. A bid must exceed the current highest bid to be accepted.
Bid acceptance needs strong consistency. Auction descriptions can tolerate delayed updates. The server determines the auction state and end time.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can create an auction with an item, a starting price, and an end time.
Users can submit bids and view the current highest bid.
The system shows bid updates. The highest accepted bidder wins when the auction ends.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: The system orders competing bids for each auction. It must keep a durable record of each bid outcome.
The scenario has 10 million concurrent auctions. Bid responses and updates must remain fast.
Retries and process failures must not lose bids. They must not reopen a closed auction or accept an outdated bid.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Auction contains the seller, item ID, starting price, end time, state, and highest bid. A version supports conditional updates.
Item contains its name, description, and image URLs. A separate item record supports a later auction for the same item.
Bid contains the auction ID, bidder, amount, time, and accepted or rejected status. A request ID can identify retries.
User identifies the seller or bidder. Payment and settlement can use a separate workflow.

sections.title: API
points: POST /auctions creates an auction and its item record. The service validates the dates and starting price.
POST /auctions/{auctionId}/bids submits a bid. A stable request ID can prevent duplicate processing after a timeout.
GET /auctions/{auctionId} returns auction and item details. Live updates deliver later changes to the highest bid.
A response must distinguish a received bid from an accepted bid. Bid history is an optional extension to the core API.

sections.title: 1) Create and view auctions
points: The API Gateway sends auction requests to the Auction Service. The service validates and stores auction and item data.
The server controls time and auction state. The countdown on the client is only a display.
The initial view returns a snapshot. Polling refreshes the highest bid. Later sections replace frequent polling with pushed updates.

flows.title: Create an auction
steps: The client sends the item, starting price, and end time to the API Gateway.
The API Gateway routes the request to the Auction Service.
The Auction Service validates the request. It stores the auction and item records in the database.
The service returns the created auction to the client.

flows.title: View an auction
steps: The client requests an auction by its ID.
The API Gateway routes the request to the Auction Service.
The Auction Service reads auction and item details from the database. It returns the current highest bid with the response.
The client polls for later changes in this initial design.

sections.title: 2) Accept bids
points: The Bid Service checks whether a bid exceeds the current highest bid. It stores the accepted or rejected result.
Keep bid history. Replacing only the highest price would remove evidence needed for audits and disputes.
The initial read followed by a write has a race condition. The consistency deep dive adds an atomic update.
The acceptance rule must also reject closed auctions and bids after the server's deadline.

flows.title: Submit a bid in the initial design
steps: The client submits a bid through the API Gateway.
The API Gateway routes the request to the Bid Service.
The Bid Service reads the highest bid from the database. It compares the new amount with that value.
The service stores the bid with an accepted or rejected status. It returns the result to the client.
This initial sequence has a race condition. The next deep dive adds concurrency control.

sections.title: 1) Strong consistency
points: Locking existing bid rows does not prevent new bid inserts. Lock one auction row instead, for a short transaction.
Redis can compare and update a cached maximum atomically. However, a cache update and a database write can fail separately.
Keep the maximum bid on the auction row to use one database transaction. Store the bid result in that transaction.
Optimistic concurrency uses the previous maximum or version as a condition. On conflict, read the current value and validate again.
A queue can order bids for each auction. A queued bid is not yet an accepted bid.
A unique request ID lets a retry return the original outcome after a lost response.

flows.title: Accept a bid with an auction-row transaction
steps: The Bid Service starts a transaction. It locks the auction row or reads its version for an optimistic update.
It compares the bid with the current maximum. The acceptance rule also checks auction state and the server's deadline.
For a valid higher bid, it updates the auction maximum. It stores the bid outcome in the same transaction.
The service commits the transaction before confirming acceptance. A version conflict requires a new read and validation.
A retried request uses its stable ID to recover the original outcome.

sections.title: 2) Durability and closing
points: A producer writes incoming bids to Kafka before the system confirms receipt. Partition by auction ID to keep their order.
The Bid Service consumes queued bids and stores their outcomes. A failed consumer can retry a retained message.
Configure persistence and replication for the required durability. Confirm acceptance only after the database commits the outcome.
Closing must use the same consistency boundary as acceptance. A delayed closing job must not permit bids after the deadline.
Define how the deadline applies to queued bids. Server receipt time and processing time can differ during a queue delay.

flows.title: Retain and process bids through Kafka
steps: The client sends a bid through the API Gateway. The gateway routes it to a producer.
The producer writes the bid to Kafka with the auction ID as its partition key.
Kafka confirms the write. The client can now receive confirmation of receipt, but acceptance is still pending.
The Bid Service consumes the bid. It validates the bid and commits the outcome in the database.
A failed consumer retries the retained message. A stable request ID prevents a second application of the same bid.

sections.title: 3) Real-time updates
points: The source design uses SSE to send highest-bid updates from the server to clients. WebSockets are another option.
Each server keeps its local client connections. Shared publish-subscribe channels deliver updates to the other relevant servers.
On reconnect, the client fetches the current auction state. An event cursor can support recovery where the event system retains history.
Compare event versions or ordering information. An old or duplicate event must not reduce the displayed highest bid.

flows.title: Push the current highest bid
steps: The client opens an SSE connection when it views the auction.
The Bid Service commits an accepted bid and the new highest value.
The server sends the updated value to its connected viewers. The final design uses publish-subscribe channels between server instances.
The client applies the update only if it is newer than its displayed state.

sections.title: 4) Scale
points: Partition Kafka and the database by auction ID. This keeps each auction's ordered operations together.
The source estimates about 15,000 bids per second at peak. Measure actual capacity before deciding the number of database shards.
Add Bid Service and Auction Service instances independently. A popular auction remains a hot key despite partitioning.
Keep the serialized bid operation short. Store stable item details in a cache, separate from the changing bid state.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Auction Service manages auction details. Kafka retains incoming bids. The Bid Service commits bid outcomes in the database.
A maximum on each auction row supports consistent acceptance. The database retains the complete bid history.
Shared publish-subscribe channels connect Bid Service instances. Each instance pushes updates to its connected clients through SSE.
Stable request IDs, atomic closure, and durable recovery records protect retries, deadlines, and failures.
